title: Otherwise God would be the author of sin, or a rational creature could commit every crime without guilt
source_text: L. Posito enim quod Deus hominem aliquem creet cum eadem ignorantia, proclivitate ad malum, & repugnantia ad bonum, cum qua jam ex Adamo nascimur; nec ulla gratia supernaturali illum juvare velit, quod fieri posse censent communiter Scholastici, homo ille nec Deum diliget, nec actus & affectus suos ad normam rectae rationis componet, sed libidini suae in omnibus indulgebit, & in diversa flagitia, prout se dabit occasio necessario ruet; ut faceret homo ex Adamo natus, si omni gratiae divinae auxilio destitueretur. Ac proinde sic Deus erit author peccati; ut qui creaverit hominem, qui nulla sua culpa, sed quali illum Deo, formare visum fuit, peccatum vitare non potest, ac quodam naturae vitio & impetu in varia scelera sese praecipitem eat, nec creatorem suum, sicuti par est, diligere valet. Vel dicendum est dari posse creaturam rationalem, quae Deum agnoscere & amare non tenebitur, quaeque poterit se omni immunditia polluere, & irae luxuriae ac gulae indulgere, stuprisque & caedibus in sui similes grassari, & reliqua patrari quae lex naturae & aeterna vetat, nec tamen propterea ullius criminis & peccati rea fiet. Quorum utrumque est vehementer absurdum; & manifestam quandam impietatem involvit.
pass_a_gloss: For supposing that God creates some man with the same ignorance, proneness to evil, and repugnance to good, with which we are now born from Adam; nor wills to help him with any supernatural grace, which the Scholastics commonly think can happen, that man will neither love God, nor compose his acts and affections to the norm of right reason, but will indulge his lust in all things, and will necessarily rush into diverse crimes, as occasion shall give itself; as a man born from Adam would do, if he were destitute of all aid of divine grace. And therefore so God will be the author of sin; as one who has created a man who by no fault of his own, but such as it seemed good to God to form him, cannot avoid sin, and by a certain vice and impulse of nature goes headlong into various crimes, nor is able to love his creator, as is right. Or it must be said that there can be given a rational creature, which will not be bound to acknowledge and love God, and which will be able to pollute itself with all uncleanness, and indulge wrath, luxury and gluttony, and rage against its likes with debaucheries and murders, and commit [so the print; read patrare, commit] the rest which the natural and eternal law forbids, and yet will not on that account become guilty of any crime and sin. Each of which is vehemently absurd; and involves a certain manifest impiety.
pass_b_english: Suppose God created a man with the same ignorance, the same leaning toward evil and resistance to good with which we are now born of Adam, and chose not to help him with any supernatural grace, as the scholastics commonly think could happen. That man would not love God or shape his acts and affections by the rule of right reason. He would give way to his desires in everything and would inevitably plunge into one crime after another as occasion arose, just as a child of Adam would do if he were left without any help from God's grace.

God would then be the author of sin, since he would have created a man who, through no fault of his own but simply because God chose to make him so, cannot avoid sin, rushes headlong into crimes of every kind by a flaw and drive in his nature, and cannot love his Creator as he ought.

Otherwise we would have to say there could be a rational creature not bound to know and love God, one that could defile itself with every impurity, give way to anger, excess and gluttony, assault its fellows with rape and murder, and do everything else the natural and eternal law forbids, and still not be guilty of any crime or sin. Both conclusions are utterly absurd and plainly involve impiety.

choices.why: The print has the passive form 'patrari' where the active 'patrare' is needed; the sense 'commit, do' is certain.
